section.title: A Prayer from the Cave
section.sectionRationale: Titled a Maskil of David when he was in the cave, this is the most explicitly autobiographical lament in the closing Davidic cluster of Book V, a short, tightly structured prayer that moves from isolation and abandonment to the bold confession, You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living, a pattern for honest prayer in seasons of total human abandonment.
section.thesis: Alone in a literal cave with no human ally in sight, David pours out his complaint without pretense, and precisely there, where no one else cares for his soul, declares the LORD his refuge and portion in the land of the living, turning isolation itself into the occasion for the boldest confession of trust.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the honest pouring out of complaint amid isolation and hidden snares, verses 1-4; and the turn to bold confession and plea for rescue, ending in praise, verses 5-7.

units.label: I pour out my complaint before Him

verses.text: I cry aloud to the LORD; I lift my voice to the LORD for mercy.
I pour out my {{siach|complaint}} before Him; I reveal my trouble to Him.
Although my spirit grows faint within me, You know my way. Along the path I travel they have hidden a snare for me.
Look to my right and see; no one attends to me. There is no refuge for me; no one cares for my soul.

units.label: You are my refuge, my portion
units.note: bold confession and plea for rescue

verses.text: I cry to You, O LORD: "You are my {{machaseh|refuge}}, my portion in the land of the living."
Listen to my cry, for I am brought quite low. Rescue me from my pursuers, for they are too strong for me.
Free my soul from prison, that I may praise Your name. The righteous will gather around me because of Your goodness to me.

siach.gloss: Complaint, meditation, or concern, spoken freely and without pretense. David does not hide his trouble from God but pours it out completely, modeling honest, unfiltered prayer even in a season of total isolation.

machaseh.gloss: Refuge, shelter, a place of safety, the same word used in Psalm 46:1. Here, surrounded by a literal rocky hideout yet abandoned by every human ally, David declares that the LORD Himself, not the cave, is his true refuge and portion.

basic.context: Composed, according to its title, while David hid in a cave fleeing King Saul, likely at Adullam or En-gedi, this short psalm captures the moment when every human support has failed and David is left with nothing but God to cry out to, and finds that God is enough.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm describes David's specific, historical experience of isolation and danger in the cave; it prescribes the abiding pattern of pouring out complaint honestly before God even in total abandonment, and of finding in Him alone sufficient refuge and portion.
basic.originalLanguages: David pours out his siach, complaint, holding nothing back from God even in the depths of isolation. He declares the LORD his machaseh, refuge, the same word used elsewhere of a sheltering cliff, fitting for a man hiding in an actual rocky cave yet trusting God, not the rock, as his true shelter.
basic.typology: David's cry from confinement, bring my soul out of prison, verse 7, anticipates both the deliverance language of Isaiah 61:1 and its fulfillment when Jesus reads that very passage and announces liberty to the captives, Luke 4:18.
basic.christ: Christ, like David, was abandoned by His closest companions in His darkest hour, no one stood with me, but the Lord stood by me, 2 Timothy 4:16-17, and His resurrection surrounds Him at last with the righteous, Hebrews 2:12, just as David anticipates the righteous gathering around him because of God's goodness.
basic.god: God is shown as refuge and portion precisely when every human refuge has failed, One who knows the way even when no one else notices or cares, and who can free a soul from the tightest prison and turn private anguish into shared praise.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 46:1 uses the same word machaseh, refuge, of God as ever-present help. 2 Timothy 4:16-17 echoes David's abandonment yet confidence that the Lord stood by him. Isaiah 61:1 and Luke 4:18 fulfill the plea to be freed from prison and brought into liberty.
basic.oneStory: David's cry from the cave, abandoned by every human ally yet confident that God alone is refuge and portion, anticipates Christ's own greater abandonment and deliverance, and promises every believer that isolation is never the last word when the LORD is the portion still held onto.

context.literary:
The psalm is built as a descent and a turn. Verses 1 and 2 speak about God in the third person: the voice goes 'to the LORD,' and the trouble is laid out 'before Him.' The Hebrew places 'before Him' in both halves of verse 2, as if the whole verse were a table on which everything is set down. Then at verse 3 the grammar changes. 'You know my way' is the first time the psalmist speaks straight to God, and from there the prayer stays in the second person. The cry becomes a conversation in the middle of a line, and the turn happens while the spirit is still faint.

The middle of the psalm is a short courtroom of loneliness. Verse 3 names the snare, verse 4 looks to the right and finds nobody standing there, and the verse closes by listing what has gone: refuge, and anyone who cares. Verse 5 answers the emptiness with a quotation: the psalmist tells God what he has said to God, 'You are my refuge, my portion.' The confession is set in the mouth of the prayer itself, so it is not a mood that arrives from outside but an act of speech made while the darkness is still real.

The last two verses are petitions with their purposes attached. Rescue is asked 'that I may praise Your name,' and the final line looks past the cave to a crowd: the righteous will gather. A psalm that began with one voice crying alone ends with a company standing around a man who was hidden. Only seven verses long, it moves from 'I' to 'You' to 'the righteous,' and it does so without ever reporting that the answer has come. The rescue is still asked for when the psalm stops, and the faith is already speaking.

The heading calls it a Maskil and a prayer. The BSB footnote notes that Maskil is probably a musical or liturgical term, so the psalm was meant to be sung and handed on, not kept as a private diary.
context.historical:
The heading ties the prayer to a cave, and Saul's pursuit of David offers two candidates. In 1 Samuel 22:1-2 David escapes from Gath and takes refuge in the cave of Adullam, where his family joins him and about four hundred men gather: the distressed, the indebted and the discontented. In 1 Samuel 24:3-4 David and his men are hiding in the recesses of another cave, at En-gedi, when Saul walks in. Psalm 57 carries a similar cave heading, so David was in more than one such place. The Judean hill country is limestone, riddled with caves, and a fugitive could vanish into one.

The situation behind the words is worse than discomfort. Just before Adullam David had fled to Gath and pretended to be insane to survive, 1 Samuel 21:10-15. After Adullam came the slaughter of the priests of Nob for helping him, a loss that touched David personally, 1 Samuel 22:18-22. He was a hunted man whose name had already cost other people their lives.

The imagery fits that hunt. A 'snare' is a bird trap, and David later describes himself to Saul as a partridge hunted in the mountains, 1 Samuel 26:20. The words 'portion in the land of the living' also carry weight in David's story. When he says that Saul's men have driven him away from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, 1 Samuel 26:19, he means that exile from the land felt like exile from the God of the land. To call the LORD 'my portion' from inside a cave was to claim an inheritance no pursuer could confiscate.

The prayer was surely sung later by people far from any cave. Israel in Babylon and the afflicted in every age had reason to make David's cave their own.
context.canonical:
Psalms 140 to 143 form a run of laments, and this one is the most bare. Psalm 140 pleads against violent men, Psalm 141 asks for protection from evil speech and the snare, and Psalm 143 will turn from the cave to the question of guidance. Psalm 142 is the floor of the sequence, the point where help seems furthest away. The whole group sits just before the praise that fills Psalm 145 and the five Hallelujah psalms after it, so the Psalter itself teaches that lament is a road into praise and not a detour from it.

The cave is a recurring place of prayer. Elijah spends a night in a cave at Horeb and tells God he is the only one left, 1 Kings 19:9-10, and God's answer is a reserve of seven thousand he had not counted, verse 18. Hebrews 11:38 remembers believers who 'hid in caves and holes in the ground' and says the world was not worthy of them. The place of hiding becomes, in Scripture's memory, a place where the faithful were being kept.

The central confession echoes through the Psalter. The Levites were given no land, because the LORD was their portion, Numbers 18:20, and psalmists make that priestly claim their own: Psalm 16:5, Psalm 73:26 and Lamentations 3:24. The pouring out of the heart is taken up in Psalm 62:8, Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 1:15 and Lamentations 2:19.

The New Testament sees the shape of this prayer fulfilled in Jesus, who proclaims liberty to captives, Luke 4:18, who was deserted by every disciple, Mark 14:50, and who 'was heard because of His reverence,' Hebrews 5:7. Paul is deserted at his first defense and yet the Lord stands by him, 2 Timothy 4:16-17.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalm was handed on as a Maskil, which suggests it was meant to teach as well as to be sung. What it teaches is a way of praying when the circumstances offer no encouragement. The author wants the afflicted to know that nothing is too raw to bring to God: the complaint, the fear, even the charge that nobody cares can be spoken aloud 'before Him.' Honesty is not the opposite of faith here. It is the form faith takes when everything else has been stripped away.

He also means the reader to notice where the prayer goes next. Having named the loneliness, the psalmist does not stay there. He reminds God, and himself, of what he has said about God: that the LORD is his refuge and his portion. Hearers who knew the Levites' story, Numbers 18:20, would catch that the king in a cave is claiming the best inheritance in Israel, one that outlasts land, crown and company.

Finally the psalm turns the private cry into public hope. 'The righteous will gather around me' tells the lonely reader that the end of the story is not solitude. The one who is shut up now will, by God's goodness, be surrounded by people who praise with him. A community that sings this psalm is learning to stand with the people in the cave, and to expect to be found there itself.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records what David felt and what he asked. It does not command anyone to feel abandoned, and it does not promise that every prayer for release from a prison, a pursuer or a depression will be answered quickly or in the way the words suggest. The cave, the snare and the pursuers belong to David's history, and the request to be brought out of prison is a request, not a guarantee.

What is plainly for us is the pattern of the prayer. It teaches us to speak to God before we speak about our troubles to anyone else, to say plainly how things look, and then to say what we believe about Him while the situation is still unchanged. It also frees us from thinking that a lament is a failure of faith. Notice, too, what the psalm does not do: it never accuses God of cruelty, and it asks for rescue so that praise can follow. Complaint that turns toward God and ends in a vow of thanks is in line with Scripture; complaint that turns away from Him is the grumbling the wilderness generation was rebuked for.

debates.question: Does 'no one cares for my soul' in verse 4 fit the fact that David's family and about four hundred men were with him, 1 Samuel 22:1-2?

views.label: It is the cry of felt abandonment, not a head count
views.case: Laments speak in honest hyperbole. A leader surrounded by a crowd can still feel that nobody carries his particular weight, and Psalm 142 is addressed to God, who knows what is literally true.

views.label: It is literally close to accurate
views.case: Those who gathered at Adullam were in distress, in debt or discontented, men who came to David for help, not to give it. None of them could stop Saul's army or answer for David's life. The verb behind 'cares' is the one meaning to seek or inquire after, so the complaint may be that no one is seeking his welfare in a way that can save him.

views.label: It belongs to a moment before the men arrived, or to En-gedi
views.case: If the psalm comes from a time when David hid in the recesses of a cave with only a few near him, 1 Samuel 24:3, the isolation is more concrete. The title does not say which cave.

debates.bearing: On every reading, the psalm gives permission for an unpolished prayer. God is not asking for a statistically accurate report of one's loneliness; He is asking to be told.

debates.question: Is the 'prison' of verse 7 a literal prison or a figure for the cave and the danger?

views.label: A figure for confinement and constriction
views.case: David was never imprisoned by Saul. The Hebrew word means a place shut in, and the cave, the snare and the pursuers together press in on him. Hebrew poetry often uses prison language for any distress that leaves no way out, as in Psalm 107:10.

views.label: A literal reference to some detention
views.case: A few readers have thought the psalm may come from a time when David was held, as at Gath, 1 Samuel 21:10-15, where he was in the hands of a foreign king. The psalm gives no detail of a cell or a guard, so this view rests on the word alone.

views.label: A prayer meant for later sufferers too
views.case: Because the psalm names no particular prison, later Israel could use it for exile or captivity. Isaiah 42:7 and Isaiah 61:1 then take up the same picture of prisoners brought out as a promise of restoration.

debates.bearing: The first and third views fit together best. David's own confinement was real but not a jail, and the broad language let the psalm serve every captive after him, up to Jesus' announcement of release in Luke 4:18.

study.originalLanguages:
Several of the verbs in this short psalm carry more than the English suggests. In verse 2 the word for 'pour out' is shaphak, the ordinary verb for pouring liquid and also for shedding blood, Genesis 9:6. Psalm 62:8 uses it of pouring out the heart before God, and Hannah uses it of herself in 1 Samuel 1:15. It is a verb of emptying: nothing is held back, and the vessel is left bare before the one who receives it. Lamentations 2:19 sharpens the image, 'pour out your heart like water in the presence of the Lord.'

The spirit that 'grows faint' in verse 3 is a reflexive form of the verb atap, to be feeble or to ebb. The same form describes the psalmist in Psalm 143:4, so the two psalms share the exact same collapse, and it is used of Jonah's life 'fading away' in the fish, Jonah 2:7. The reflexive form describes a spirit that is giving way from the inside, not one being pushed.

Verse 4 is a study in lost shelter. 'No one cares' translates a phrase built on the verb darash, to seek or to inquire after. It is the verb for the land the LORD 'cares for,' Deuteronomy 11:12, and for the scattered sheep that have 'no one to search for them,' Ezekiel 34:6. The 'refuge' that has gone is manos, a place to flee to; Jeremiah 25:35 says 'flight will evade the shepherds.' Verse 4 therefore mourns that there is nowhere to run, and then verse 5 answers with a different noun, the refuge of God Himself.

'My portion' is cheleq, a share in a division. It is the word of the Levites' arrangement in Numbers 18:20, and psalmists repeat it in Psalm 16:5 and Psalm 73:26. 'Prison' in verse 7 is masger, from the root meaning to shut, and Isaiah 42:7 uses the same noun of the dungeon from which prisoners are brought out.

The verb in 'the righteous will gather around me' is unusual. It is usually taken as 'surround,' but it is related to the word for a crown, and Proverbs 14:18 uses the same form of the prudent being 'crowned' with knowledge, so some hear a note of honour in it: the righteous ringing him like a crown. The final clause, 'because of Your goodness to me,' uses gamal, to deal with someone, here a good dealing, as in Psalm 13:6.

typology.type: The cave and the closed tomb
typology.fulfillment: David, anointed king but not yet enthroned, is hidden in a cave while the reigning authority hunts him, and from that place a company begins to form around him, 1 Samuel 22:1-2. The pattern returns in Jesus, whose body was laid in a tomb cut into the rock and sealed with a stone, Matthew 27:60, and from whom the new people of God would be gathered after the resurrection. Lazarus's tomb, 'a cave with a stone laid across the entrance,' John 11:38, shows the same imagery in a miniature of that hope. The type falls short because David never died in his cave; Christ really entered death and came out of it.

typology.type: The distressed who gather around the hidden king
typology.fulfillment: The people who came to David were the distressed, the indebted and the discontented, and he became their leader, 1 Samuel 22:2. Jesus draws the same kind of crowd, Luke 15:1-2, and says He came for the sick and not the healthy, Mark 2:17. In Him the broken are made brothers, and He is not ashamed to call them that, Hebrews 2:11-12. The escalation is moral and eternal: David trained an outlaw army for Saul's overthrow, while Christ forgives and remakes His people, and His kingdom is not advanced by the sword, John 18:36.

typology.type: The LORD as portion, and driven from the inheritance
typology.fulfillment: David protested that Saul's men had driven him from sharing in the inheritance of the LORD, 1 Samuel 26:19, yet in the cave he calls the LORD his portion. Jesus took this to its end. He had 'no place to lay His head,' Luke 9:58, and gave up everything, and in Him believers are qualified to share in the inheritance of the saints, Colossians 1:12, an inheritance that is imperishable and reserved in heaven, 1 Peter 1:4. The pattern holds in the psalm only in part: David's inheritance was a land, while the portion Christ gives is God Himself and a world made new.

typology.type: Bring my soul out of prison
typology.fulfillment: The request in verse 7 is answered at its deepest level in Jesus, who reads Isaiah's words about proclaiming liberty to the captives and says they are fulfilled in Him, Luke 4:18-21. He shared flesh and blood so that He might free those 'held in slavery by their fear of death,' Hebrews 2:14-15. David's own deliverance was from Saul and was temporary; he still died. The release Christ gives is not from a pursuer but from sin and death, and it is final.

study.christ:
The New Testament never quotes this psalm by name, so the link to Christ runs by pattern, and the pattern is strong. David is the anointed king rejected by the sitting king, hunted, hidden, and deserted. Jesus is the anointed one rejected by the leaders of His people. In Gethsemane His soul was 'consumed with sorrow to the point of death,' Mark 14:34, and He prayed with the very honesty of this psalm, asking that the cup pass and then yielding to the Father's will, verses 35 and 36. Hebrews says that in His earthly days He offered up prayers and petitions 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death,' Hebrews 5:7. That is David's 'I cry aloud' and 'I pour out' taken to the limit.

Then came the emptiness of verse 4. When Jesus was arrested 'everyone deserted Him and fled,' Mark 14:50, exactly the bleakness of 'no one attends to me,' and He had told them that this would happen, John 16:32. He adds, 'Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.' Where David asks God to look to his right and see that no one stands there, Jesus knew that His real company was the Father. Later, Stephen sees Him standing at the right hand of God, Acts 7:55-56, and Paul says He is there interceding, Romans 8:34. The One who was left without an advocate on earth has become the advocate of the lonely, Psalm 109:31.

The psalm also points ahead to what He wins. The ending of verse 7 promises a gathering of the righteous around the one who was shut up, and John 12:32 has Jesus say that when He is lifted up He will draw everyone to Himself. The people He draws are those who, like David's men, come with debts, distress and discontent. Isaiah 53:12 says the Father will allot Him a portion with the great because He poured out His life to death.

A fair caution applies. We should not make every line of the psalm into a word of Christ, since David also speaks as a sinner needing rescue. The strongest use is the simplest one: because Jesus knows what this psalm describes from the inside, Hebrews 4:15, the person praying it is praying to a high priest who has been there.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is that He is a listener of the first rank. He receives the whole of a man's complaint without rebuke, and nowhere in the psalm does He correct David's tone. The God of Scripture is not threatened by honest anguish. Hannah, Jeremiah and Job say the same kinds of things before Him, and He answers them with presence rather than with offence.

Second, the psalm shows a God who knows. 'You know my way' is the heart of verse 3, and it is said exactly when the psalmist cannot see the way himself. Psalm 139:1-3 gives the doctrine in full, that He searches out our path and is aware of all our ways, and here it appears as comfort. The snare is hidden from David but not from God, and the God who sees the trap is the same God to whom David is speaking. That knowledge is personal, not distant. It is the knowledge of a shepherd who goes looking for the lost, the very thing no one in David's world was doing, Ezekiel 34:6.

Third, God is shown as sufficient in a way that goes beyond help. David calls Him 'my portion,' which makes God the share itself and not merely the giver of shares. For a man cut off from home, throne and people, this is the claim of a Levite: the LORD is the inheritance, Numbers 18:20. It is a doctrine of God's own self-giving. The psalm holds two truths that look unlike each other: God is the believer's whole portion, and yet the believer is hungry, hunted and hidden. Scripture never resolves that tension by denying either side. It gives the believer a prayer that can carry both.

Fourth, God is shown as the source of community. The final verse credits the gathering of the righteous to the LORD's goodness, gamal, His good dealing, not to David's cleverness or charm. God does not simply rescue individuals; He builds a company of praise around those He rescues.

There is a lesson for worship too. A church that sings only victory misses what this psalm teaches: that a cave can be a sanctuary, and that a voice raised from the floor of the world is among the sincerest praise God hears, Psalm 62:8.

crossReferences.note: The likely setting. David escapes to the cave of Adullam, his family come down to him, and about four hundred distressed, indebted and discontented men rally around him. The psalm's lonely complaint is set beside this crowd, which shows that 'no one cares' is the cry of someone no human company can really help.

The other cave candidate, at En-gedi, where David and his men hide in the recesses while Saul enters. The scene shows the psalm's second half in action: David trusts God to be his refuge and does not seize the chance to take matters into his own hands, which makes his prayer for rescue more than a wish.

David says Saul's men have driven him from sharing in the LORD's inheritance and that the king is hunting him like a partridge. It explains why 'my portion in the land of the living' is such a bold line and why 'snare' fits a hunted man.

Elijah in a cave at Horeb says he is the only one left and that they seek his life. The parallel of cave, complaint and sense of isolation is plain, and the answer, a remnant of seven thousand in verse 18, shows the sort of correction a loneliness like David's may need.

The LORD tells Aaron that He is the portion and inheritance of the priests. David takes the Levite's privilege and claims it in a cave, which shows what 'portion' meant: the whole of a person's inheritance was God Himself.

Asaph says God is the strength of his heart and his portion forever, even when his flesh and heart fail. It develops what Psalm 142 states in the middle of the crisis, that the portion is not lost when the body and spirit give way.

Hannah says she has poured out her soul before the LORD, and her words use the same verb as 'I pour out my complaint.' Her story shows that such prayer, even when it looks like despair from outside, is heard and answered.

The shepherds' failure is that there is no one to search for the scattered sheep. It sets the sharp phrase 'no one cares for my soul' in the larger frame of God's promise to be the shepherd who does seek His people, which Jesus claims in John 10.
The Servant is to bring prisoners out of the dungeon, using the same noun for a shut-in place as 'prison' in verse 7. It shows how the psalm's request was read as a promise of a coming deliverer.

Paul at his first defense: no one stood with him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him. Paul prays this psalm in action, left alone and finding that the Lord Himself is the refuge that verse 5 confesses.

Jesus offered prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death. It joins this psalm's 'I cry aloud' and 'I pour out' to the supreme prayer of Gethsemane, showing the Lord who shares the cry.

study.oneStory:
Genesis opens with the observation that it is not good for the man to be alone, Genesis 2:18. Psalm 142 sits in the world after the fall, where that aloneness has become real. In the garden Adam hid from God among the trees, Genesis 3:8; Cain complains that from God's face he will be hidden and will be a fugitive and a wanderer, Genesis 4:13-14. The first hiding was an escape from God. David's hiding is the reverse: he is hidden from his enemies, and he brings the whole matter to God. Where the first pair avoided His presence, the psalmist runs to it.

The pattern is the pattern of the Bible's redemption. Israel groaned in Egypt, and 'God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant,' Exodus 2:23-24. The cry of the hidden and the oppressed is where each stage of rescue begins. David's cave is one scene in that long line, and it points to the decisive one. The king whose throne is promised in the Davidic covenant waits in a cave before he reigns; the Son of David waits in a tomb. In both the loneliness is real, and in both God had not left His servant.

The church lives between those scenes. Hebrews remembers the faithful who hid in caves and holes in the ground, Hebrews 11:38, and the New Testament assumes that God's people will often look as David did, few, afflicted and nearly forgotten. Paul, deserted at his first defense, knew that the Lord stood by him, 2 Timothy 4:16-17.

The story ends in a world where the psalm's last line has come true on the largest scale. A multitude too large to count stands before the throne, Revelation 7:9-10, so the righteous gather indeed. The portion David claimed is given in full: God Himself is with His people as their God, and they will see His face, Revelation 21:3 and 22:4. The prisoner is brought out, the snare is gone, and no one will hide again.

quiz.q: What does the title of this psalm tell us about its setting?

options.text: It was written by David when he was in the cave, likely while fleeing King Saul.
options.note: The title, A Maskil of David, when he was in the cave, points directly to David's flight from Saul, 1 Samuel 22 or 24.

options.text: It was written by David during a time of peace and prosperity in Jerusalem.
options.note: The title specifically locates the psalm during a cave hiding, a season of danger, not peace or prosperity.

options.text: It was written after David became king over all Israel.
options.note: The cave setting reflects David's fugitive years before his kingship, not his later reign.

options.text: It was written by an anonymous exile in Babylon.
options.note: The title attributes the psalm to David specifically in a cave, not to a later, anonymous exile setting.

quiz.q: What does David do with his trouble in verse 2?

options.text: He pours out his complaint before God and reveals his trouble to Him fully.
options.note: David models complete, honest disclosure of his distress directly to God.

options.text: He hides his trouble from God out of shame.
options.note: The verse describes the opposite, complete openness with God about his trouble.

options.text: He only complains to his human companions, not to God.
options.note: The complaint is explicitly directed to God, before Him, not merely to people.

options.text: He pretends everything is fine and suppresses his real feelings.
options.note: The psalm is marked by unusually honest, unfiltered expression, not suppression of feeling.

quiz.q: What does David observe about his human support in verse 4?

options.text: That no one attends to him, no refuge remains, and no one cares for his soul.
options.note: This stark statement of isolation captures the emotional depth of David's felt abandonment.

options.text: That he is surrounded by an army of loyal soldiers.
options.note: The verse expresses the felt absence of human support, not the presence of an army.

options.text: That King Saul has become his ally.
options.note: Saul is David's pursuer in this narrative, not an ally; the verse expresses isolation, not reconciliation.

options.text: That his family has come to rescue him.
options.note: The verse specifically states that no one cares for his soul, the opposite of rescue by family.

quiz.q: What bold confession does David make in verse 5?

options.text: "You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living."
options.note: This declaration turns David's isolation into an occasion for confident trust in God alone.

options.text: "I have no hope left in this cave."
options.note: The verse is a confession of confident trust, not despair without hope.

options.text: "My own strength will save me from Saul."
options.note: David explicitly turns to God as refuge, not to his own strength.

options.text: "I will abandon my trust in the LORD."
options.note: The verse affirms trust in the LORD as refuge, the opposite of abandoning that trust.

quiz.q: What does David anticipate happening once God rescues him, according to verse 7?

options.text: That his soul will be freed from prison so he may praise God, and the righteous will gather around him because of God's goodness.
options.note: David expects his personal deliverance to become an occasion for shared praise among the righteous.

options.text: That he will keep his deliverance completely private and never mention it to anyone.
options.note: The verse anticipates public praise and gathering of the righteous, not private silence.

options.text: That he will take revenge on Saul once free.
options.note: The verse focuses on praise and communal gathering, not revenge against his pursuer.

options.text: That he will remain hidden in the cave permanently.
options.note: The verse anticipates rescue and freedom from confinement, not permanent hiding.

questions: David pours out his complaint to God without pretense, holding nothing back. Is there a trouble you have been hiding from God rather than pouring out honestly before Him?

David feels that no one attends to him or cares for his soul, even though, historically, others were nearby. Where do you feel isolated right now, and how does it help to know God receives that feeling honestly rather than requiring you to first prove it accurate?

In his lowest, most isolated moment, David declares, You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living. What competes with God for the place of your refuge and portion when life feels like a cave?
David asks God to free his soul from prison so that he may praise God's name. What confinement, physical, emotional, or spiritual, are you asking God to free you from right now?

David expects that his personal deliverance will draw the righteous around him in shared praise. How might sharing your own story of God's help become an encouragement to others facing similar isolation?

translationNotes.note: A Maskil is probably a musical or liturgical term whose precise meaning is uncertain, used as a heading for several psalms including 32, 42, 44-45, 52-55, 74, 78, 88-89, and this one.
Look to my right and see reflects the ancient custom of a defender or advocate standing at a person's right hand; David observes that no such defender is present for him.

Portion in the land of the living echoes the language used of the Levites' inheritance in Numbers 18:20, where the LORD Himself, not land, is their portion, language David applies personally to his own circumstance.
